title: Top 100 Pennies Worth Money in 2026, With Real Auction Prices
summary: Top 100 pennies worth money, each with a real graded auction price and date: 1793 Chain cents, 1909-S VDB, 1943 copper, the 1955 doubled die, modern finds.
body_markdown:
Almost every penny you own is worth one cent. The exceptions come down to a specific date, a mint mark, a die variety or a mistake at the Mint, and then to grade, which matters more than anything else. At the very top sits a 1793 Chain cent:[PCGS MS66, $2,350,000 at Heritage in January 2015](https://www.pcgs.com/auctionprices/details/1793-chain-periods-ms/91342) , the highest auction price of any penny on this list. The famous 1943 copper penny exists too. The lone Denver example made $840,000 at auction in 2021.


Below are the top 100 pennies worth money, from the first cents of 1793 to a 2017 Shield cent, each with a dated sale in a stated grade and a straight answer on whether one could turn up in a jar.


On the prices: nearly all of them were read from[PCGS Auction Prices](https://www.pcgs.com/auctionprices) on September 29, 2026. A "record" is the highest result PCGS has logged for that coin in any grade, which almost always means one exceptional Mint State coin. Where a worn example turned up at auction or in the PCGS Price Guide, it's there too, since that's the number closer to a jar find. These are past sales of particular coins. They say nothing about what yours is worth; grade and authenticity decide that.


## The 10 highest auction prices on this list


Eight of the ten were struck before 1805. The other two are 1943 bronze cents.

## Early cents, 1793 to 1909: where the seven-figure records live


The early cents own the top of every ranking, and almost none of them will ever surface in a jar. Look at the 1795 Reeded Edge. Graded VG10, a heavily worn coin, it still brought $1,265,000 in 2009, because only a handful are known. When the supply is that small, wear barely matters.


Indian Head cents are friendlier. A common 1887 in Good 4 is a $3 coin on the PCGS guide. The 1877, the key to the series with 852,500 struck, is $650 in the same grade, and a gem one hit $149,500 in 2007. Worn Indian cents of ordinary dates can still turn up in old accumulations; the keys almost never do.

## Wheat cents, 1909 to 1958: the 1909-S VDB and 29 more


Inherited a coffee can of old cents? Read this section slowly. The Wheat cent run is where a key date can hide in a pile of common ones, and the gap between worn and gem is enormous. A 1909-S VDB in VF30 sold at Stack's Bowers for $660 in 2018. A red MS67 went for $170,800 in January 2026. Same date, same mint mark, roughly 260 times the money.


The 1914-D and the 1922 No D are both widely counterfeited, so get either one authenticated before you believe it. Several common dates, the 1918 and 1935 among them, carry big PCGS records thanks to one superb coin each. We left those out. Listing them would suggest an ordinary 1918 is valuable, and it isn't.

## Memorial and Shield cents, 1959 to now: the ones still in circulation


Pocket change is a live source here, along with a few of the errors further down. Most of the finds are varieties, not dates: a doubled die, or a reverse with the wrong spacing between the A and M of AMERICA. The money is smaller too. A 1983 doubled die reverse in MS65 red sold for $247.52 on eBay in 2018, and PCGS now calls a[1995 doubled die in MS65 red "a $45 coin"](https://www.pcgs.com/news/the-1995-doubled-die-lincoln-cents) .


That $45 is the realistic guide figure for most modern finds. The big figures in the table mostly belong to coins at MS66 and above, a level few pennies from a cup holder reach.

## Errors, off-metal strikes and proofs: the 1943 copper and its relatives


Errors are the penny videos' favorite subject, and the 1943 copper is the coin the fakes copy. The 1943 bronze story is true: the Mint switched the cent to zinc-coated steel that year, a few leftover bronze blanks went through the presses anyway, and fewer than two dozen are known across all three mints. The 1944 steel cents are the same mistake run backwards, a leftover steel blank struck the year the Mint went back to copper alloy.


The generic errors at the bottom of the table are the realistic ones. PCGS puts[most slabbed off-center Lincoln cents from 1959 to 2001 at $40 to $100](https://www.pcgs.com/news/two-exciting-options-for-collecting-off-center-coins) , with about ten scarcer dates at $200 to $500. Fun to own. Not a windfall.


One row here has no price at all. The Mint says 1974 aluminum cents can't be lawfully owned, and the one that came to auction in 2014 was pulled and handed back.

## What the viral penny prices trace back to


### The 1999 penny "worth $4,500"


An ordinary 1999 cent is worth a cent. The variety behind the headlines is the 1999 Wide AM, a circulation cent struck with a proof-style reverse, where the A and M in AMERICA sit clearly apart. It's a legitimate variety, and it does turn up in change. The sales we could actually read: $192 for a PCGS MS66 RD at Stack's Bowers in September 2018, and $200 for a PCGS AU58 BN on eBay in March 2023.


We couldn't confirm a $4,500 sale for any 1999 cent on a page we could open. PCGS's page for the plain 1999 cent does list a $138,000 top result, from Heritage in 2006. That lot appears to be a 1999 cent struck with a Roosevelt dime reverse, a[mint error of the same family as the 2001-D mule](https://coinweek.com/rare-lincoln-cent-roosevelt-dime-reverse-mule-worth-100000-or-more/) , and nothing like a normal 1999.


### The $2.3 million penny


It's the 1793 Chain cent, Periods variety: PCGS MS66, $2,350,000, Heritage, January 2015. A lot of posts hang the big number on the 1943 copper penny instead. The closest verified figure there is the[$1.7 million private sale of the 1943-D bronze in 2010](https://www.pcgs.com/news/pcgs-certified-1943-d-bronze-cent-sold-for-17-million) . Since it's unique, that's the same coin Heritage sold for $840,000 in 2021.


### Four-figure prices on ordinary modern cents


Some of the scariest numbers come straight off PCGS's own pages, which log eBay sales alongside auctions. The highest 2017-P result shown there is $4,500. The coin behind it was graded NGC PO1 RD and sold on eBay in 2018. PO1 is Poor 1, the bottom of the grading scale, and RD means full red, a pairing that is odd on its face. A PCGS MS67 RD 2017-P went for $74.95. The 2019-W reverse proof has the same pattern: a $5,000 eBay high next to normal PR70 RD sales of $86 and $172.50.


The penny videos high in search results, with titles along the lines of "retire if you find this," quote numbers like these. Check the grade behind any figure they use. And the hype has happened before: 1995 doubled dies briefly topped $500 during that year's media frenzy, then fell once collectors learned hundreds of thousands existed.


## How to check a penny from your jar


Start with the date and the mint mark. On Lincoln cents a D (Denver) or S (San Francisco) sits under the date (a few recent collector-only cents carry a W), and Philadelphia cents carry no letter at all,[the 2017-P aside](https://www.pcgs.com/news/whats-that-letter-p-doing-on-my-cent) . Match what you have against the tables. A 1909-S is interesting. A plain 1909 mostly isn't, unless the reverse has VDB at the bottom.


Doubling next, with a 10x loupe: LIBERTY, IN GOD WE TRUST and the date, looking for a second outline offset from the first. That's what makes a 1955 or a 1972. On 1998, 1999 and 2000 cents, flip the coin and check the gap between the A and M of AMERICA.


### The 1943 magnet test, and what it misses


Normal 1943 cents are steel, and steel sticks to a magnet. A genuine 1943 bronze cent doesn't. Simple enough, except the fakes come in two kinds. One is an ordinary steel 1943 plated with copper, and the magnet catches it. The other is a cent from another year, usually 1945, 1948 or 1949, with the date altered to read 1943. That coin really is bronze. It won't stick, and the magnet tells you nothing.


For those, look hard at the 3.[CoinWeek notes](https://coinweek.com/1943-d-lincoln-copper-cent-a-collectors-guide/) that on a genuine 1943 bronze cent it's identical to the 3 on a steel cent, and that the typical fake is an altered date. Run the magnet the other way on 1944: a true 1944 steel cent should stick, and a "1944 steel" that doesn't isn't steel. So the magnet can rule a coin out, but it can never prove one genuine.


### Weigh it: 3.11 grams or 2.5


Bronze cents weigh 3.11 grams. The copper-plated zinc cents that replaced them during 1982 weigh 2.5, per[PCGS](https://www.pcgs.com/news/looking-for-those-lincoln-memorial-cent-small-dates) . Any scale that reads tenths of a gram will separate them, and that's how the 1982 bronze Small Date and the rare 1983 cents on leftover bronze blanks get found: a 1983 that weighs about 3.1 grams may be struck on one, per[Numismatic News](https://www.numismaticnews.net/us-coins/1983-copper-cent-error-fetches-30000) . A genuine 1943 bronze cent should also weigh 3.11. Steel cents run about 13% lighter.


Then grade and color, the part that decides most of the money. Coins are graded 1 to 70, and copper gets a color call on top: RD for red, RB for red-brown, BN for brown. On the PCGS guide an 1887 Indian cent is a $3 coin in Good 4 and a $350 coin in MS65 brown, and nothing separates the two but wear.


## Think you found one? Authenticate it before anything else


Hold it by the edge and put it somewhere soft. Don't clean it. Cleaning leaves hairlines a grader spots right away, and on copper it can strip the original color that the RD and RB designations depend on.


Then send it to PCGS or NGC for authentication and grading. CoinWeek's line on 1943 coppers is that no coin valued over $500 should be bought or sold without authentication, and it's a sensible bar for every key date and error in this list. Grading is paid per coin, so compare the fee with the numbers in these tables before you send in a BIE like the one that sold for $15.50.

## Penny questions people ask


### What are the top 20 most valuable pennies?


The first ten are in the table near the top. Numbers 11 through 20 on this list, by auction record: the 1944-S steel ($408,000), the 1823 large cent ($376,000), the 1943 bronze from Philadelphia ($372,000), the 1799/8 ($368,000), the 1958 doubled die ($336,000), the 1793 Wreath with lettered edge ($293,750), the 1909 VDB matte proof ($258,500), the 1856 Flying Eagle ($192,000), the 1944 steel ($180,000) and the 1909-S VDB ($170,800).


Only one of the twenty, the 1958 doubled die, was struck after World War II.


### How much is a 1943 steel penny worth?


Not much, in the grades most people have. Philadelphia alone struck 684,628,670 of them, and[PCGS says](https://www.pcgs.com/news/bronze-1943-lincoln-cent) steel 1943s are common in average circulated grades and only collectible in pristine Mint State. Be wary of very shiny ones sold as "brilliant uncirculated." Some steel cents have been stripped and replated; collectors call them reprocessed. The 1943 that brings serious money is the bronze one, and it won't stick to a magnet.


### Which years of pennies are worth money?


For modern cents, no year is valuable across the board; it's a date plus a mint mark, variety or error. For coins that can still turn up in change, the years to check are 1970 (S mint, Small Date), 1982 (bronze Small Date), 1983, 1984, 1995, 1998, 1999, 2000, 2009 and 2017 (P mint), each for the specific variety in the modern table. In an old jar, the Wheat cent keys are the 1909-S VDB, 1914-D, 1922 with no mint mark, 1931-S and the 1955 doubled die.
